**Reading map:** Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning* (2020), Chapter 11 §11.1. All examples are newly authored.

## Motivation

Delivery times may contain different operational regimes: short local orders and longer routes. A single Gaussian can miss two clusters. A mixture combines component densities without requiring known group labels.

## Derivation and notation

$$
p(t)=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\,\mathcal N(t\mid\mu_k,\sigma_k^2),\quad \pi_k\geq0,\quad\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1
$$

Read this model together with the distributional, geometric or optimisation assumptions. An equation without its domain of validity is not a complete explanation.

## Apply it to our running example

Start with two components, one centred at 10 minutes and one at 20, each with variance 16 and weight 0.5. For a 9-minute order, the low-time Gaussian has much greater density than the high-time Gaussian, so its posterior membership probability is larger.

## Constraints and interpretation

Components are probability distributions, not necessarily real customer segments. Switching the numeric labels of components leaves the mixture density unchanged (label switching).

## Your turn

Why must the mixture weights sum to one? What distribution results if K=1 and pi1=1?
